comparator.sourceNotes: The regular-entry Greek and Latin pathway closes 60+60+60, assuming the published prior classical-language preparation; an adapted entry curriculum is not stacked on top. Diagnostic test, ACASA orientation and recurring tutoring are mandatory zero-credit formation. Current evidence supports Dutch and English instruction; Greek and Latin remain studied/read languages absent teaching-medium evidence. The joint-degree change begins in 2027-2028 and does not alter current identity.

trace: examines the rise, organisation and fall of major empires, including Rome, and the theories used to explain imperial power
traces warfare in the western world from Greek hoplites and Roman legionnaires onward, covering the military organisation of the ancient societies studied in the cultural-history strand
trains students in primary-source and archival historical research and in writing up an independent source-based study
introduces the Western philosophical tradition from the ancient Greeks onward, supplying the ancient philosophical material and the argumentative technique the programme builds on
works through virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism from their historical sources, including the ancient ethical theories read in the philosophy strand
examines how influential Western thinkers theorised human nature, society and political authority, beginning with the classical political philosophers
introduces the material culture of ancient societies from the Near East to classical Athens and Rome, reading artefacts and production techniques as evidence about the communities that made them
studies the archaeology of community and political decision-making in early-democratic Greece directly from its material remains
reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built and how it was expressed in myth, religion, art, literature and architecture, and traces how that heritage was later remembered
examines how a humanities discipline writes its own history and trains art-historical research, visual analysis and academic writing
reads ancient epic and myth, from Homer and Virgil to the Mahabharata and Byzantine and Arabic romance, and follows how those narrative traditions travel into later cultures
develops practical criticism and literary interpretation, establishing the formal analysis of literary texts that the programme applies to classical material
surveys canonical literary works chronologically from the epic of Gilgamesh onward, including the ancient texts that shaped the Western literary tradition
analyses how literary texts are reworked in a different medium, giving concrete method for studying the afterlife of canonical narratives
applies competing interpretive perspectives to literary texts in an independent research project, which is the research training this programme uses in place of a thesis
teaches classical rhetorical theory and practice from Plato, Aristotle and Quintilian and the construction of persuasive argument
analyses in detail the linguistic choices that create meaning in texts, a stylistics descended directly from the third canon of classical rhetoric
puts classical rhetorical theory into practice through public speaking, debate and storytelling in a community-engaged setting
extends classical rhetoric and argumentation theory into contemporary models of framing and persuasion across public discourse
studies and practises poetic form, from traditional lyric to experimental verse, as the creative rewriting counterpart of the programme's reception strand
traces Western art from the early Renaissance onward, the period in which classical forms and subjects were deliberately revived, and trains visual analysis
studies Renaissance Italy and the wider Mediterranean, the setting in which classical antiquity was recovered and reused
analyses pre-digital media objects, including early printed books, and how their material properties shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge
sets out legal, social and normative perspectives on law and surveys constitutional, criminal, international and private law, giving the legal vocabulary this programme needs
surveys the modern period from 1815, the era in which popular sovereignty, nationalism and classical political models were argued over in the terms the programme examines
examines human rights both as positive law and as a historical and philosophical construction, the modern counterpart of ancient arguments about who belongs to a political community
covers the sources of international law together with the use of force, armed conflict and refugee law, the contemporary legal frame for questions of movement and membership
compares how five constitutional orders establish government, sovereign powers and civil rights, giving the comparative method for reading ancient constitutional arrangements
works through private law, the field whose categories of persons, obligations, property and contract descend from Roman law
surveys EU fundamental rights, citizenship and the free movement of persons, the most direct modern legal counterpart to ancient citizenship and mobility arrangements
supplies the analytical tools for comparing political systems and explaining how they function and change
introduces the schools of international-relations theory and applies them to historical and contemporary cases of power between polities
examines how a composite political order exercises public authority and turns competing interests into policy
examines the causes and dynamics of violent and nonviolent conflict and the conditions for lasting peace across history, sociology, political science and law
trains qualitative research design, fieldwork and interpretive data analysis for studying how people make sense of their social and political world

alternatives.label: Classical antiquity through literature, rhetoric, philosophy & archaeology
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response combines classical literature and myth in translation, rhetoric and stylistics, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, imperial history, material culture and the reception of antiquity. It is a related-fields programme and cannot reproduce the comparator’s cumulative Greek and Latin language, linguistics, translation and original-text sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is organised around classical literature and myth, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, imperial history and the later reception of antiquity. The label states those related fields and does not imply Greek or Latin proficiency.
progression: Introductory literary studies, classical rhetoric, Western philosophy and world archaeology are placed in the first year, before the 200-level work on Greek archaeology, stylistics, myth and epic, empires and ancient warfare, and before the third-year courses on ancient democratic heritage, persuasive communication, adaptation, interpretive theory, art-historical research and the archival research seminar. No scheduled course carries a formal prerequisite, every course is offered in its assigned term, and the one 100-level course placed in year two, Introduction to Western Art History, is a deliberate entry point into the Renaissance reception strand rather than a displaced foundation.

alternatives.label: Antiquity, democracy & the politics of the present
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different question-led route centred on how ancient arrangements of democracy, citizenship, empire and political membership shaped later societies. It connects the material and intellectual history of antiquity to comparative politics, law, conflict and historical research rather than organising the curriculum around literary interpretation.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum uses archaeology, empire and ancient political philosophy as its starting point, then concentrates on law, comparative politics, international relations and modern historical research. The label reflects that question-led structure rather than presenting it as a Classics degree.
progression: Law, Society & Justice, political philosophy and Western philosophy open the first year and Law, Society & Justice precedes every law course that formally requires it. World archaeology, Greek archaeology, public international law and ethics follow in semester two; comparative politics, modern history, empires and human rights in semester three; and the 300-level work on private law, EU politics, ancient democratic heritage, peace and conflict, EU law, historical research and art-historical research in years three. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every course is offered in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: The alternatives differ by twelve courses / 90 EC in each direction. The closest response concentrates on literature, rhetoric, stylistics, creative reception and art history, while the second replaces that block with a coherent sequence in law, comparative politics, international relations, conflict and modern historical inquiry. The substitutions follow from the evidenced democracy-and-political-reception question.
traceOverrides: examines how Western thinkers from the classical political philosophers onward theorised political authority and the good community, which is the question this programme carries into the present
studies the archaeology of community and collective decision-making in early-democratic Greece, giving this programme its material evidence for how an ancient democracy actually worked

reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built, how ancient commentators attacked it as too inclusive and too emotional, and how that contested heritage has been reused since, which is this programme's central case
examines how empires rise, hold and lose power, placing Rome alongside later imperial formations that invoked it
reads ancient myth and epic comparatively and follows how those narratives were carried into later cultures that used them to explain their own political order
trains archival and primary-source historical research, the method this programme uses to test claims about how the past is invoked in present-day argument

selection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The first is the closest feasible response through classical literature in translation, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, archaeology, history and reception. The second uses the programme’s evidenced continuing influence of antiquity to build a substantively different political, legal and historical curriculum; twelve courses / 90 EC differ in each direction. A third programme centred on Greek and Latin language, philology, translation and original-text expertise is not feasible because the current UCR workbook contains no ancient-language sequence, Greek or Latin linguistics, or advanced original-text seminars. That central disciplinary gap remains explicit rather than being filled with general literature or communication courses.

notes.text: The Greek and Latin Language and Culture programme combines cumulative Greek and Latin language acquisition, linguistics, translation and advanced reading of classical, late-antique and medieval texts in the original with literature, history, philosophy and material culture. UCR can approach classical antiquity through literature in translation, rhetoric, philosophy, archaeology, heritage, history, law and politics, but it does not teach Greek or Latin. The UCR programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than a full Classics curriculum.

The external programme follows a fixed Greek-and-Latin disciplinary sequence, alongside 30 EC of approved profiling and a 12-EC thesis. UCR assembles related material across individually selected literature, communication, heritage, philosophy, history, law and politics courses; it has no separate ancient-language sequence, profiling block or scheduled thesis. Optional independent research is shown only as the standardized comparison element.
